finding.claim: Password change requires no current password or re-authentication and sets a fixed password, enabling account takeover by anyone holding a session.
finding.source: Any authenticated session; request body ignored

trace.note: login_required checks "uid" in session, aborts 401 otherwise
set_password is a stub; impact depends on implementation (unverified)

finding.guards_checked: login_required session-presence check only. No current-password check, no re-auth, no input validation, no CSRF check.

verdict.guard_found: login_required at routes.py:11-12 aborts with 401 when "uid" is absent from the session, so anonymous callers are blocked. No re-authentication or current-password check exists, and none is needed for the refutation.
verdict.reason: The trace is accurate (routes.py:41-44, login_required at 11-12, stub at 52), but the attacker must already hold a logged-in session, and set_password(g.uid, ...) at routes.py:44 only acts on that session's own uid, so the caller already has control over that account and no privilege boundary is crossed. The missing re-auth and the hardcoded "hunter2" are real hardening issues, but as stated they do not give anyone power they lack; the "account takeover" framing is overstated.

finding.claim: Hardcoded password literal "hunter2" used as the new credential, violating the org policy against hardcoded credentials; same pattern for hardcoded email at line 37.
finding.sink: New password value passed to set_password at routes.py:44
finding.guards_checked: None. Value is visible to anyone with source access and is a predictable credential for every account this endpoint affects.

verdict.guard_found: login_required (routes.py:8-16, abort(401) at line 12) gates /settings/password at line 42 but only requires a session; it does not block the hardcoded value. No CSRF or other check appears in routes.py. set_password (routes.py:52-53) is a no-op stub, so the constant is never validated or overridden.
verdict.reason: routes.py:44 always sets the caller's password to the literal "hunter2" regardless of input, and routes.py:42 only requires a logged-in session, so anyone who knows the constant can log in as any account that has triggered the endpoint (via a session-holder or a CSRF-style trigger). The email at routes.py:37 is not a credential, and "every account" overstates the scope, which is limited to the session's own uid.
